title: Which AI has the best sense of humor?
excerpt: 16 frontier models rated jokes humans had already rated. Here's how often each model agreed with the people.

Can a judge rank comedians?

Picking the winner of one pair and ranking whole systems are different jobs. Here each judge scored 5,028 pairs from the SemEval-2026 MWAHAHA competition, where about a hundred annotators ranked 31 joke-writing systems.

Good at pairs and good at ranking are different skills

Each dot is a judge. Up the page: agreement with people on single pairs. Across the page: how closely its ranking of the 31 systems matches the human ranking. Hover a dot for its name.

LL judge 1Frontier models

Does a smarter model judge humor better?

We put each model’s general-ability score from the LMArena text leaderboard against its agreement with people here.

Smarter models tend to be better judges of humor (correlation +0.42 on a scale from -1 to +1)

Across the page: LMArena text score (21 Aug 2026). Up the page: overall agreement with people. Our judge is a humor-only fine-tune with no LMArena entry, so it is left off. Hover a dot for its name.

Other findings

  • More thinking does not help. In separate runs we tried the higher reasoning settings on Gemini 3.7 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5 and both Kimi models. None improved and several got worse, so every judge on this page ran at the lowest setting its provider allows.
  • The best generator is a weak judge. Claude Opus 5 leads the Humor Arena as a writer and lands near the bottom here, on pairs and on ranking alike.
  • Intelligence helps, moderately. Across the 15 frontier models, the LMArena text score and agreement with people correlate at +0.42 on a scale from -1 to +1 (rank correlation +0.30): a real but loose link, and with 15 models the uncertainty is wide. The top LMArena model, Claude Fable 5, sits mid-table here, so a high general score is no guarantee.
  • Undecided pairs are common. Most judges change their pick on 15 to 30% of pairs when the jokes swap sides. Mistral Medium 3.5 flips on more than 40%.

Methodology

The judge panel

Every current flagship we could reach on 25 Aug 2026, the previous release where one is still served, and our own judge.

LL judge 1, our own model

  • What it is. A large open model fine-tuned to pick the funniest jokes, trained on 1,822 head-to-head votes from readers of our apps. It answers without explanation or reasoning.
  • What it was checked against. A panel of 51 raters who never trained it: on the pairs where it commits to an answer, it agrees with that panel more often than an extra human rater does (72% against 52%).
  • Where it stops. It declines to pick on about a quarter of pairs, and it is poor at ranking whole systems, so we route that job to a frontier model.
  • None of these pairs were in its training. Every test on this page was checked for overlap against everything it was trained on.

The tests

Each test is a list of joke pairs written for the same brief, with a human answer key. Sizes: mixed 239 pairs, clean 786, dark 147, frontier jokes 280 (167 with a human side), curated 281, ranking 5,028.

TestWhat it isAnswer key
Mixed239 same-brief pairs from our own apps, clean and dark mixedHuman majority, median 11 votes
Clean786 clean same-brief pairsHuman majority, at least 5 votes
Dark147 dark same-brief pairsHuman majority
Frontier jokes280 pairs of jokes written by frontier models for the Humor Arena, 167 with a human side5 votes each from 51 raters who never trained our judge
Curated281 pairs: a real joke against a deliberately plausible weaker oneOne editor, no crowd
Ranking5,028 decisive pairs from SemEval-2026 MWAHAHA, 31 systemsThe organizers’ human leaderboard

How the test was run

  • LLM and human judges never saw the author, model name, or vote count.
  • Every pair was shown twice with the jokes swapped, so a judge that follows screen position counts as undecided.
  • A judge scores 1 for picking the human side, 0 for the other side, 0.5 when its two answers disagree.
  • One prompt for every model, reasoning at the lowest level each provider allows, all run on the same day.

Caveats

We built the judge that wins most of these tables, so here is where the deck is stacked and where it is not.

  • Home advantage. The mixed, clean and dark tests come from our own apps and largely the same readers whose votes trained our judge, and our judge answers in the format it was trained on while the frontier models got one untuned prompt. The frontier-jokes test is the fair one: 280 pairs of jokes written by the Humor Arena models, voted on by 51 raters who never trained our judge. Our judge scores 67.7% there and leads the best frontier models by 3 to 6 points, with overlapping intervals. Treat the frontier numbers as a floor.
  • Ties and refusals. An undecided pair counts as half right for every judge, and a refused pair is dropped rather than scored wrong. On the pairs our judge commits to, its agreement is higher still, so the tie rule does not manufacture its lead.
  • Humans disagree too. On the closest calls two people agree with each other only about 54% of the time, and two halves of the same panel agree on about 80% of pairs overall, so no judge can approach 100%. Scores from a single day carry about two points of noise. Treat smaller gaps as ties.
  • Not about joke writing. This page says nothing about which model writes the funniest jokes. That is the Humor Arena.

Other findings

  • More thinking does not help. In separate runs we tried the higher reasoning settings on Gemini 3.7 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5 and both Kimi models. None improved and several got worse, so every judge on this page ran at the lowest setting its provider allows.
  • The best generator is a weak judge. Claude Opus 5 leads the Humor Arena as a writer and lands near the bottom here, on pairs and on ranking alike.
  • Intelligence helps, moderately. Across the 15 frontier models, the LMArena text score and agreement with people correlate at +0.42 on a scale from -1 to +1 (rank correlation +0.30): a real but loose link, and with 15 models the uncertainty is wide. The top LMArena model, Claude Fable 5, sits mid-table here, so a high general score is no guarantee.
  • Undecided pairs are common. Most judges change their pick on 15 to 30% of pairs when the jokes swap sides. Mistral Medium 3.5 flips on more than 40%.

LL judge 1, our own model

  • What it is. A large open model fine-tuned to pick the funniest jokes, trained on 1,822 head-to-head votes from readers of our apps. It answers without explanation or reasoning.
  • What it was checked against. A panel of 51 raters who never trained it: on the pairs where it commits to an answer, it agrees with that panel more often than an extra human rater does (72% against 52%).
  • Where it stops. It declines to pick on about a quarter of pairs, and it is poor at ranking whole systems, so we route that job to a frontier model.
  • None of these pairs were in its training. Every test on this page was checked for overlap against everything it was trained on.

How the test was run

  • LLM and human judges never saw the author, model name, or vote count.
  • Every pair was shown twice with the jokes swapped, so a judge that follows screen position counts as undecided.
  • A judge scores 1 for picking the human side, 0 for the other side, 0.5 when its two answers disagree.
  • One prompt for every model, reasoning at the lowest level each provider allows, all run on the same day.

注意事项

We built the judge that wins most of these tables, so here is where the deck is stacked and where it is not.

  • Home advantage. The mixed, clean and dark tests come from our own apps and largely the same readers whose votes trained our judge, and our judge answers in the format it was trained on while the frontier models got one untuned prompt. The frontier-jokes test is the fair one: 280 pairs of jokes written by the Humor Arena models, voted on by 51 raters who never trained our judge. Our judge scores 67.7% there and leads the best frontier models by 3 to 6 points, with overlapping intervals. Treat the frontier numbers as a floor.
  • Ties and refusals. An undecided pair counts as half right for every judge, and a refused pair is dropped rather than scored wrong. On the pairs our judge commits to, its agreement is higher still, so the tie rule does not manufacture its lead.
  • Humans disagree too. On the closest calls two people agree with each other only about 54% of the time, and two halves of the same panel agree on about 80% of pairs overall, so no judge can approach 100%. Scores from a single day carry about two points of noise. Treat smaller gaps as ties.
  • Not about joke writing. This page says nothing about which model writes the funniest jokes. That is the Humor Arena.
